extra.message: Insecure Pickle Deserialization enabling RCE — Remote code execution — attacker can execute arbitrary Python code on the server [verified: Same as finding 2: pickle.loads deserializes attacker-controlled bytes enabling RCE through crafted pickle object reconstruction.]

Arbitrary Python eval with sandbox escape — Remote code execution — attacker can bypass restricted eval and run arbitrary Python code [verified: Same as finding 1: eval with empty __builtins__ on user expr is bypassable; attacker can recover builtins and achieve RCE.]

Arbitrary code execution via Python eval on user-controlled expression — Attacker can execute arbitrary Python code on the server by crafting an eval expression that escapes the restricted globals, enabling file read, command execution, or full server compromise. [verified: Same as finding 1: eval() with restricted __builtins__ on user-controlled expr is bypassable via Python introspection, enabling RCE.]

Jinja2 Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) — Remote code execution — attacker can escape the Jinja2 sandbox and execute arbitrary Python code [verified: Same as finding 3: Jinja2 Template constructed from user fragment GET parameter enables SSTI with arbitrary code execution.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 — Remote code execution on the server. Attacker can execute arbitrary Python code and read sensitive data from the application context and filesystem. [verified: Same as finding 3: user fragment interpolated into Jinja2 Template string with no sandbox, served as text/html, enables SSTI-RCE.]

OS Command Injection via ping host parameter — Remote code execution on the server — attacker can run arbitrary OS commands as the application user [verified: Same as finding 0: os.system() concatenates unsanitized user host parameter into shell command; no input validation or shell escaping.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 fragment parameter — Remote code execution, sensitive data disclosure (environment variables, SECRET_KEY, database credentials), and full server compromise. [verified: Same as finding 3: Jinja2 Template('Result: ' + fragment).render() enables SSTI-to-RCE, output as text/html.]

Server-side template injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 user-controlled template fragment — Attacker can execute arbitrary code on the server through Jinja2 template injection, accessing Python internals, reading sensitive files, and achieving remote code execution. [verified: Same as finding 3: Jinja2 Template string built from user fragment enables SSTI with arbitrary Python code execution, served as text/html.]

Server-Side Template Injection (Jinja2 SSTI) — Remote code execution or sensitive data disclosure through template engine sandbox escape; output served as HTML enabling reflected XSS. [verified: Template('Result: ' + fragment).render() concatenates user 'fragment' into a Jinja2 template string with no sandbox; output served as text/html enabling full SSTI with RCE via object traversal.]

Hardcoded Default Django SECRET_KEY — Session hijacking via forged cookies, CSRF bypass, and bypass of all Django cryptographic signing protections if deployed with the default key. [verified: The default `'django-insecure-change-me'` at line 13 is a publicly documented Django fallback key enabling session/cookie forgery when SECRET_KEY is unset; no alternative safeguard is present.]

Weak default Django SECRET_KEY — If the SECRET_KEY env var is not set in production, an attacker can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, and password reset tokens, gaining full account takeover on any user. [verified: The `os.getenv('SECRET_KEY', 'django-insecure-change-me')` at line 13 uses a well-known default that breaks all Django cryptographic signing when the env var is absent; no compensating control exists.]

Cross-tenant data access via client email change in profile form — A client can change their email to impersonate another client, gaining unauthorized access to that client's legal matters, confidential documents, and attorney-client messages — a complete cross-tenant data breach. [verified: User.email has no unique constraint (confirmed in migration), ProfileUpdateForm exposes email with no duplicate check, and all client-access helpers resolve identity via Client.objects.get(email=request.user.email) string match. A client can change their own email to another client's and transparently access that victim's matters, documents, and messages.]

Missing rate limiting on login endpoint — Brute-force password guessing enabling unauthorized account access [verified: Identical to finding 0: no rate-limiting is applied to CustomLoginView; brute-force attacks face no throttling or lockout.]

CSRF on user_toggle_active allows attacker to enable/disable user accounts via GET — An attacker can disable legitimate user accounts (denial of service) or re-enable previously-disabled accounts (potential unauthorized access) by tricking a logged-in firm_admin into visiting a crafted page. [verified: user_toggle_active performs a state-changing DB write (user.save()) with no @require_POST or method check; the template renders it as a plain <a href> GET link, and Django's CsrfViewMiddleware does not validate GET requests, allowing CSRF via a crafted page.]

NoSQL Injection in MongoDB query passthrough — Arbitrary MongoDB data access, potential authentication bypass, and data exfiltration [verified: Same as finding 4: JSON body passed directly to MongoDB find_one() enables injection of $where, $regex, $ne operators.]

XXE via XML External Entity Injection — Local file disclosure, server-side request forgery, and potential denial of service through entity expansion (billion laughs). Client identity resolved by unenforced email matching instead of FK relationship — Cross-client data access: users sharing an email or attackers manipulating their email can access another client's matters, documents, and messages. Cross-Client Data Access via Email Matching (IDOR) — Horizontal privilege escalation allowing a client to access another client's confidential legal matters, documents, and communications by matching their email to the victim client's email. IDOR via Email-Based Client Identity Resolution — A client user can escalate to access another client's confidential legal matters, documents, deadlines, tasks, and messages by changing their email address. BOLA — attorney can create privileged notes on matters they do not lead — An attorney can inject arbitrary privileged notes into any other attorney's matters, enabling data pollution, misdirection, and potential abuse of the privileged-notes trust boundary. IDOR in privileged note creation bypassing matter-level access control — An attorney with no assignment to a matter can create privileged notes on it and view the matter title, gaining unauthorized access to confidential case data and injecting content into matters they shouldn't have access to. [verified: Same privileged_note_create issue as finding 3: the view fetches a Matter by user-supplied pk at line 19 without calling can_access_matter(), letting any attorney create privileged notes on matters they do not lead and view the matter title.]

Missing Matter‑Scope Authorization in Client Message Creation — An attorney can inject auto‑approved, client‑visible messages into matters they do not belong to by manipulating the matter parameter, leaking information to the wrong client and triggering spurious notifications to the matter's assigned attorney. IDOR via Email-Based Client Identity Matching in Task Access Control — A client user can change their profile email to match another client's email, then access and enumerate tasks belonging to matters of the impersonated client, leaking confidential legal task details. [verified: The can_access_task function at tasks/views.py:120 resolves client identity via Client.objects.get(email=user.email), and the ProfileUpdateForm at accounts/forms.py allows any authenticated client user to change their own email with no uniqueness validation (User model has no unique=True on email, no clean_email override). User Enumeration via Login Error Message — Attackers can enumerate valid usernames in the system by observing distinct error messages for disabled vs. non-existent accounts. [verified: Identical to finding 1: the distinct 'Your account has been disabled.' message for valid-but-disabled users versus the generic invalid-credentials message enables username enumeration.]

Account enumeration via login response differentiation — Attacker can enumerate valid usernames by distinguishing 'disabled account' from 'invalid credentials' responses, facilitating targeted password attacks. [verified: In form_valid(), the check 'if not user.is_active_account' returns a distinct message 'Your account has been disabled.' before super().form_valid() runs, while invalid credentials produce Django's generic error, allowing an attacker to distinguish valid-but-disabled accounts from nonexistent ones.]

CSRF via State-Changing GET on Notification Mark-Read Endpoint — An attacker can force an authenticated user to mark specific notifications as read without their knowledge or consent by tricking them into visiting a malicious page. [verified: View notification_mark_read at accounts/views.py:141-146 performs state-changing notif.save() on any HTTP method (accepts GET) with only @login_required—no method restriction, no CSRF check. Django's CsrfViewMiddleware ignores GET requests, and SameSite=Lax (Django 5.0 default, not overridden in settings.py) still permits cross-site top-level navigations, allowing an attacker-crafted link to mark ]

API client document endpoint leaks cross-client document metadata via missing matter scope — A client user can enumerate and retrieve metadata for client-shared documents belonging to other clients' legal matters, exposing confidential matter numbers, document titles, categories, and associated matter identifiers across the entire firm. [verified: api_documents for clients (api/views.py:62-63) filters only visibility='client_shared' without matter__client scope; client_documents in documents/views.py:158 correctly adds matter__client=client, so cross-client document metadata (title, category, matter __str__) is exposed.]

Cross-Client Document Metadata Leak via API - clients can enumerate other clients' shared documents — A client user can discover the existence, titles, categories, and associated matter IDs of documents shared with other clients, violating client data isolation across the system. [verified: api_documents client path (api/views.py:63) omits the matter__client filter present in documents/views.py:158; serialize_qs converts the matter FK to its __str__ (matter_number: title), exposing other clients' matter identifiers and document metadata.]

CSRF via State-Changing GET on Deadline Completion Endpoint — An attacker can silently mark deadlines as completed on behalf of authorized users by tricking them into loading a crafted URL, disrupting deadline tracking and potentially causing missed court dates. [verified: Same CSRF-on-GET vulnerability as finding [1]: `deadline_complete` (line 85-95) performs state change with no method guard, allowing an attacker to complete deadlines via crafted link when an authorized victim clicks it.]

IDOR via client identity resolution by email string matching — Potential cross-user access to documents, matters, deadlines, and tasks if emails collide or change [verified: Both User.email (migration 0001, no unique constraint) and Client.email (migration 0001, no unique constraint) lack uniqueness, and client identity is resolved by bare string match via Client.objects.get(email=user.email) across all views; email changes on User accounts are never propagated to Client records, enabling stale cross-user access, though .get() on non-unique Client.email limits collisi]

Missing authentication on ops endpoint — Unauthenticated access to internal operational data and case metadata [verified: Same as finding 6: case_client_fold_108 has no _wrk_gate or @login_required, returning operational data unauthenticated.]

Open Redirect via user-controlled redirect target — Phishing attacks, OAuth token theft, and social engineering via crafted redirect URLs [verified: Same as finding 7: redirect() with unvalidated user lane parameter from GET/POST enables phishing via crafted external URLs.]

Sensitive Authorization header logged in plaintext — Credential and token leakage through log files enabling account takeover [verified: Same as finding 9: Authorization header logged at WARNING level in plaintext exposes ops token to anyone with log access.]

Unbounded Memory Allocation via User-Controlled Count Parameter — Denial of service via memory exhaustion, causing application crashes and unavailability. [verified: Same as finding 25: unbounded count parameter drives range() list comprehension enabling server memory exhaustion.]

Permissive CORS with credentials echoing untrusted Origin — Cross-origin attacks with credentials, session hijacking via malicious websites [verified: Same as finding 11: Origin reflection with credentials=true allows any origin to make authenticated cross-origin requests.]

Missing HTTPS Enforcement — No SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT or HSTS Configuration — In production, users may access the application over unencrypted HTTP, exposing all traffic including session cookies, CSRF tokens, and sensitive legal data to network interception and man-in-the-middle attacks. [verified: settings.py has SecurityMiddleware but omits both SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT (defaults to False) and SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS (defaults to 0, HSTS disabled); no reverse-proxy configuration or SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER exists anywhere in the repo to compensate, so the application will serve all traffic over plain HTTP in production, exposing session/CSRF cookies (despite the Secure flag on cookies when DEBUG=Fal]

Unauthenticated Access to Uploaded Legal Documents in DEBUG Mode — Unauthenticated access to confidential legal documents including contracts, pleadings, evidence, and privileged communications stored under MEDIA_ROOT. [verified: Same underlying vulnerability as finding [0]: the static() helper on line 21 (imported at line 4) serves all uploaded legal documents without auth when DEBUG=True, and no compensating control (middleware, view wrapper, or filesystem permissions) protects these paths.]

Unauthenticated access to uploaded legal documents via DEBUG static serve — Unauthenticated access to all uploaded legal documents, evidence, and discovery files [verified: The static() call at line 21 serves MEDIA_ROOT files (including DocumentVersion.file uploads) at /media/ URLs with zero authentication when DEBUG=True, bypassing the @login_required and can_access_document() access controls present on the normal document_download view.]

Mass Assignment of Sensitive Financial Fields via MatterForm — Non-admin users (attorneys, paralegals) can modify retainer amounts and billing notes on matters, bypassing intended financial controls. Missing Matter‑Scope Authorization in Client Message Approval — An attorney or paralegal from Matter A can approve client messages belonging to Matter B, making them visible to Matter B's client and triggering notifications, bypassing matter‑level access controls and potentially leaking confidential communications to the wrong client. CSV formula injection in spreadsheet exports — If an attacker can inject formula characters into exported fields (e.g., via matter.title or matter_number), opening the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application can execute arbitrary commands or exfiltrate data from the victim's machine. HTTP Response Header Injection via Content-Disposition filename — HTTP header injection enabling response splitting or download path manipulation [verified: Same unsanitized version.file_name interpolation into Content-Disposition header as Finding 1 (line 129), additionally enabling path-traversal download suggestion manipulation via ../../../ sequences in the uploaded filename; no filename sanitization exists at upload or download.]
